name: PT Kino Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Kino Indonesia — a real earnings recovery that the price already carries
frontmatter.summary: Kino's first half doubled operating profit and the balance sheet is deleveraging, but at ten times our forward earnings the market has already paid for it. Our DCF is close to the price and the illiquidity haircut takes the target below it. We start at HOLD.
thesis: Kino is a challenger FMCG house: beverages, personal care, food, pet food and pharmaceuticals, with a controlled owner and a public float of about one share in seven.
The 2026 half-year is an actual, not a promise, but it is now in the price: the shares trade at a forward multiple in line with the larger staples names on earnings that contain a one-off.

Restating D&A from the notes rather than the data pack turns EBITDA into a coherent number; on that measure FY2025 interest-bearing debt was three point seven times EBITDA against a four-times covenant, so the leverage test clears its limit by only a quarter of a turn and the relief obtained from the banks names the current ratio, not a comfortable balance sheet.
Deleveraging is the clearest company-specific upside and it is in our base case: debt has fallen for two years and we model repayment continuing, so the interest line shrinks every year.

The sweetened-beverage excise from H2-2027 lands on more than half of sales with the rate unset; that, plus a thin float, is why the probability-weighted value after the liquidity discount sits below the price.

catalysts.event: Nine-month 2026 results — whether the second-quarter operating margin holds through the third quarter
FY2026 audited accounts and the FY2027 dividend proposal
Implementing regulation for the MBDK excise — the rate and the sugar threshold
First half-year of the excise regime (targeted start H2-2027)
First covenant test after the balance-sheet date, on the FY2027 accounts

blocks.text: **Rating HOLD, twelve-month target Rp1,345, total return -9.5% against Rp1,570.** The build is shown in full because the target is not a single number: the base DCF is Rp1,524 a share, rolled forward one year at the cost of equity to Rp1,645; the bear, base and bull cases at 25.0%, 55.0% and 20.0% weight to Rp1,682; the house illiquidity discount of 20.0% then takes it to Rp1,345. The discount, not the operating view, is what turns a small fundamental premium into a negative expected return.

Kino Indonesia is a mid-cap Indonesian consumer-goods group: beverages, personal care, food, pet food and pharmaceuticals, sold under local brands (Ellips, Eskulin, Sleek, Cap Kaki Tiga, Master, Ristra) through general and modern trade [S3]. It is a challenger, not a leader: the group competes with Indofood, Wings, Mayora and Unilever across categories and does not disclose a market-share number, saying only that it is focused on strengthening domestic share through price-competitive products and a wide distribution network [S3].

What the market pays today is the recovery. FY2025 was the first clean year after the FY2022 loss: sales of IDR4,421.6bn, gross margin 43.6%, EBIT IDR213.1bn and net profit attributable to owners IDR123.7bn, with earnings per share of Rp90 [S3]. The first half of 2026 broke away from that base: sales grew by more than a fifth year on year, operating profit roughly doubled and net profit attributable to owners nearly tripled, and that is the last reported actual rather than a forecast [S0]. Our FY2026 forecast reproduces it: revenue of IDR5,239.5bn, EBITDA of IDR598.0bn and earnings per share of Rp153 [S0].

The variant view is narrow and uncomfortable: the recovery is real, and it is priced. The shares trade at 10.3x our FY2026E earnings and 10.6x FY2027E, and at 5.7x EV/EBITDA against the peer median shown in the valuation section; on cash the business yields 8.0% of free cash flow to equity. That is not expensive for a staples name, but it is not the discount the recovery story implies either. Our DCF value of Rp1,524 is close to the price, and the float — 13.5% public with a further 3.5% in treasury — costs a fifth of that value to own. We would rather be early than wrong, but there is no margin of safety here.

Three things move the value. First, whether the operating margin holds: the first half's cost ratio was materially better than FY2025's, and our FY2026 EBITDA margin of 11.4% assumes most of that step is permanent [S0, S3]. Second, the pace of repayment: interest expense was IDR129.3bn in FY2025 and we model it falling to IDR80.9bn by FY2030 as debt is repaid [S0]. Third, the excise: the government has committed to a tax on sweetened packaged drinks from the second half of 2027, on a business where beverages are 53.0% of revenue, and the rate is not yet set [S4, S3].

Kino Indonesia manufactures and sells consumer goods in five reporting segments. Beverages take 53.0% of revenue, personal care 36.7%, with food, pet food and pharmaceuticals making up the rest [S3]. The portfolio is brand-led rather than category-led: Ellips hair care, Eskulin and Sleek personal care, Cap Kaki Tiga and Panther beverages, Kino Candy and Snack It in food, and Ristra in health [S3]. Production is in-house, and the FY2025 report gives installed capacity and volumes by segment: personal-care production of 13,420 kl against installed capacity of 84,259 kl, beverages at 287,934 kl and food at 11,490,232 kg [S3]. That capacity position matters for the investment case: the group can grow volumes a long way before it needs to spend on new plant, which is why capex can track D&A in the near term.

The operating footprint is Indonesian with a set of export and overseas entities: Kino International in Singapore, Kino Care in Malaysia, Kino Consumer Philippines, Kino Vietnam, Linanda in India and Kino Japan, plus a joint venture with PT Bina Indo Nawasena [S3]. Sales are routed through general trade and modern trade, and the annual report's account of the distribution system — an in-house distributor application rolled out across the whole network, e-procurement and e-budgeting — points to a business that competes on reach rather than on a single blockbuster brand [S3].

The strategy the board set for 2026 is defensive and incremental: new product launches, process efficiency, better-targeted promotion and stronger distribution channels, with information systems as an enabler [S3]. Management framed the outlook as cautious optimism, expecting performance growth in line with Indonesia's economic growth rate [S3]. The first half delivered far more than that, which tells you either that the plan was set conservatively or that the second half gives some of it back. Our forecast assumes the former partially and the latter partially: we do not extrapolate a first half that included a favourable non-operating line, but we do not round the growth back to GDP either.

Ownership and group structure are covered in the governance section; the short version is that the founder's holding company controls 79.0% of the shares and the founder is also president director [S3], so this is a controlled company with a small public float rather than a widely held mid-cap. The company employs 4,847.0 people and carries a market capitalisation of IDR2,164.7bn at Rp1,570 [S0].

Indonesian consumer staples is a volume game in a young, urbanising population with a long tail of traditional retail. Growth in any single year is a function of three things: nominal household consumption, the split between volume and price, and input costs — sugar, palm derivatives, wheat, packaging and the rupiah. The company's own discussion of 2026 points to domestic demand carrying the industry while export demand slows on trade friction, and to cost pressure, currency and changing consumer preference as the things to watch [S3].

Our sector deck prices the inputs rather than the demand. The agri deck has CPO at US$1,240/t for FY2027E against a spot of US$1,180/t, so the basket our cost link uses is broadly flat to slightly up; wheat, corn and soymeal follow similar paths [S3]. We use CPO as a proxy for the palm-derived surfactants and glycerine in personal care and for plastic packaging across the portfolio, with a fifth of cost of goods sold exposed and four-fifths of any move passed into prices (the financial section explains the calibration). The macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD to the dollar and the policy rate at 5.75%, both of which matter here: the debt is short-term bank debt that reprices, and part of the input bill is imported [S3].

Indonesian FMCG has historically been a premium-multiple sector: the large listed staples names traded at
high teens to low twenties earnings multiples for most of the last decade, and the past several years have
been a de-rating story rather than an earnings story for several of them. The relevant base rate for a
mid-cap challenger is therefore not "will it grow" but "what multiple will the market still pay once the
recovery is in the numbers". We treat the multiple as a constraint on the target, not as a source of it.

Regulation is where the industry view becomes company-specific. The government has committed to a tax on sweetened packaged drinks (MBDK) from the second half of 2027, has written a revenue target into the 2027 budget, and is still deciding both the rate and the sugar-content threshold that would trigger it; the finance ministry's customs director general said in October 2026 that the technical rules were being completed and that implementation was targeted for that half [S4]. For Kino this lands on the largest segment. The mitigating facts are that the regulation has been postponed repeatedly — the budget committee chair noted it had already been delayed three years — that a sugar-content basis leaves room to reformulate, and that the industry will pass what it can into prices [S4, S3].

Competitive position: Kino is a challenger in every category it operates in. In personal care it competes with Unilever and Wings; in beverages with Mayora, Wings and Indofood's beverage arm; in food with a long list of local producers. Its edge is distribution density and brand breadth rather than pricing power in any one category, and the annual report's own account of the moat is distribution through general and modern trade plus continuous product launches [S3]. Five-forces view: supplier power is moderate and rising with commodity prices, and the company dual-sources raw and packaging materials to manage it [S3]; buyer power is high in modern trade and low in traditional retail; the threat of substitutes is high in beverages, where private label and reformulated drinks compete on price; rivalry is intense and mostly on promotion, which is why selling expense runs above a third of revenue [S3]; and new entry is constrained by distribution and brand spend rather than by capital. Regulation is the swing external influence, followed by the rupiah.

**The restatement that matters.** The Yahoo data pack's D&A line for FY2025 is not the depreciation charge; it is about a quarter of it. The charge is disclosed in four parts, and the parts add up: property, plant and equipment depreciation of IDR168.1bn in total across cost of goods sold, selling expense and administrative expense [S3, F35], right-of-use depreciation of IDR11.7bn in selling expense and IDR16.9bn in administrative expense [S3, F20, F21], and intangible amortisation of IDR7.3bn [S3, F22] — together the restated D&A of IDR204.0bn. FY2024 is built the same way, from IDR161.3bn of PPE depreciation, IDR17.4bn and IDR17.5bn of right-of-use depreciation and IDR10.4bn of amortisation, for IDR206.6bn [S3, S5]. The effect is not cosmetic: EBIT does not change, but EBITDA becomes IDR417.2bn, the EBITDA margin becomes 9.4%, and that is the measure the lenders' interest-bearing-debt test uses — on it FY2025 debt is three point seven times EBITDA against the 4.0x limit, a margin of a quarter of a turn on our measure rather than the wide cushion the unreconstructed pack would suggest [S3]. It also reframes the covenant story in the risk section, but not into comfort: the waiver disclosures name the current ratio, and CIMB, OCBC and BCA describe the relief only as non-fulfilment of FY2025 financial covenants, so the LK does not establish that the leverage test was untouched — on our restated EBITDA it clears the limit with a quarter of a turn to spare, which is not much.

**Revenue.** FY2025 sales of IDR4,421.6bn grew only 1.2% on FY2024, held back by a soft first half; the mix was beverages and personal care, with pet food the fastest growing small segment [S3]. The 2026 first half changed the trajectory: sales grew by more than a fifth on the prior-year half, which on our full-year assumption of 18.5% growth implies the second half decelerates on a tougher comparative base, because FY2025's second half was the stronger one [S0, S3]. Our FY2026 forecast is IDR5,239.5bn. Beyond that we fade to mid-single-digit nominal growth, with FY2027 held at 8.0% because the excise lands mid-year on the beverages segment [S4].

**Margins and costs.** Gross margin was 43.6% in FY2025 and 43.3% in our FY2026 forecast; the first half printed essentially the same number as the full prior year, so the assumption is not an expansion, it is the last actual repeated [S0, S3]. The margin recovery is all in the cost base: selling plus administrative expense ran at IDR1,712.5bn in FY2025, while the ratio in the 2026 first half was materially lower because promotion and sales-force costs did not grow with revenue [S3, S0]. We hold that achieved ratio, which is the single largest reason our FY2026 EBITDA margin of 11.4% sits above FY2025's 9.4% — a step a reviewer should test against the audited second half.

**Below the operating line.** The arithmetic is a bridge, not an assertion. In FY2025, EBIT of IDR213.1bn less net interest of IDR129.3bn against interest income of IDR1.9bn, plus other income of IDR72.7bn, gives pre-tax profit of IDR158.4bn [S0, S3]. The other-income line includes foreign-exchange gains, a trademark impairment charge and disposal items the company groups as non-operating [S3]. The same bridge for our FY2026 forecast is EBIT of IDR357.0bn, net interest of IDR113.2bn, other income of IDR26.1bn and pre-tax of IDR271.8bn [S0]. The half-year actual matters here and we state it plainly: in the 2026 first half, pre-tax profit sat BELOW EBIT by the net interest charge, with only a small positive other-income item — which is why our other-income assumption is the annualised H1 run-rate in FY2026 and nil thereafter [S0]. Because that one-off disappears, FY2026 net profit of IDR210.9bn is above FY2027's IDR203.4bn even though operating profit rises; on a clean basis FY2027 grows.

The interest line uses the rate the company actually pays, 7.2%, on the opening debt balance [S3, S0]. The discount rate in the valuation section uses the marginal market rate instead; the two are reconciled there, and we do not hide the gap by averaging them. We model net repayment from the observed deleveraging: debt fell to IDR1,561.3bn in FY2025 and to a lower balance again at the June 2026 sheet, and we carry repayment of IDR-144.0bn in FY2027 tapering to IDR-60.0bn by FY2030 [S0, S3]. That is the company's own behaviour repeated, not an upside we have invented, and it is why cash does not pile up earning a deposit rate below the cost of debt.

**Cash flow and working capital.** FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR632.2bn against net profit of IDR125.9bn — cash conversion several times earnings, with the difference explained by the restated D&A and by a working-capital release as payments to suppliers fell [S3]. The accruals screen is therefore clean: this is the opposite of the pattern that worries us, earnings running ahead of cash. The caveat is that the release does not repeat. We model operating working capital at 8.0% of sales, between the FY2025 level of IDR455.8bn and the June 2026 position, which was already far lower [S0, S3]. Because the first forecast year is a half-year stub measured from 30 June, the model's full-year working-capital swing would otherwise put a release into H2 that has already happened; we correct the stub in the valuation bridge so that H2 carries the build to the 8.0% target from the June position, and the forecast change from FY2027 on is the ordinary build at the stated growth rate [S0].

Capex was IDR208.1bn in FY2025, 4.7% of sales, up sharply on FY2024 as the group bought plant [S3]. We hold capex near D&A while growth is absorbed by existing capacity, then lift it above D&A from FY2029: at a terminal return on capital in the low teens, the growth we forecast has to be paid for with reinvestment, and a capex-equals-D&A terminal would be growth for free.

**Balance sheet and debt.** Net debt was IDR1,437.6bn at FY2025, 3.4x the restated EBITDA, and it fell again by the June 2026 balance sheet [S0, S3]. The debt is mostly short-term bank lines plus current maturities of long-term loans [S3]; it is refinanced rather than amortised, which is normal for Indonesian mid-caps but means the interest line is sensitive to the policy rate. The covenants in the short-term loan notes are a minimum current ratio of 1.0x, interest-bearing debt to equity of no more than 2.5x, interest-bearing debt to EBITDA of no more than 4.0x and a debt-service cover ratio of at least 1.0x, tested annually at the year-end [S3]. FY2025 current assets of IDR1,580.5bn against current liabilities of IDR2,375.9bn were below the current-ratio test, and the company obtained waivers from four banks for the FY2025 test date — CIMB, CTBC, OCBC and BCA — between 20 February and 30 March 2026 [S3]. That is a liquidity flag, and we treat it as one. The leverage test at the same date was not breached but was close: interest-bearing debt of IDR1,561.3bn against restated EBITDA of IDR417.2bn, three point seven times against the 4.0x covenant, leaving a quarter of a turn of headroom [S3, S0]. On our FY2026 forecast the balance improves — net debt to EBITDA falls to 2.1x and interest-bearing debt to EBITDA to about two and a half times — so the leverage line is not the binding constraint in the forecast, but the current-ratio test is the one to watch and the FY2025 headroom means a weak second half would matter. Equity of IDR1,746.3bn includes a revaluation surplus; for any price-to-book work the pre-revaluation equity is the right denominator, and we do not use price-to-book as a valuation leg for that reason [S3].

**Capital allocation.** The dividend has been ratcheted: Rp22 a share for FY2023, Rp32 for FY2024 and Rp45 for FY2025, a payout of 50.2% of net profit in the last year and about half the year before [S3, S0, S5]. What we hold is the payout ratio, not the rupiah amount: 49.6% of earnings in the forecast, which on our higher earnings lifts the dividend to Rp76 a share and gives a yield on today's price of 4.8% [S3]. The dividend and debt repayment are funded from free cash flow; there has been no equity issuance, and a treasury stake of 3.5% is held [S3]. If the company cancelled those treasury shares, earnings per share and the dividend per share would rise without any change in the business — an unvalued optionality we flag rather than model.

**Earnings-quality flags, run as a pre-thesis gate.** The accruals ratio is strongly negative in the good sense, with cash far above earnings [S3]. Receivables are not outgrowing revenue — the working-capital movement in FY2025 was a release, not a build [S3]. There is no capitalised development cost of consequence and no provisioning game of the kind that matters in a non-financial of this shape. IDX regime status: we found no special-monitoring-board or special-notation flag in the filings or the news we reviewed [S2, S3]. Related-party flows are small: other payables to PT Royal Bintang Persada, an entity under common control, for lease and interest expense, were IDR7.5bn against total liabilities of IDR2,722.2bn [S3]. Structure flags: the auditor is a mid-tier firm rather than a Big Four practice [S3]; no share pledge is disclosed in the annual report or the announcements we reviewed [S2, S3]; there has been no rights issue, private placement or discounted issuance since listing, and none is pending [S3, S2]. That matters because a discounted placement to an affiliate is the standard IDX channel for transferring value from minorities, and this company has not used it. Nothing here is manipulation-class; the float is a liquidity flag, not a governance one.

Kino is a consumer staples compounder, so the value of the business is the present value of the cash it will generate after the reinvestment needed to keep growing. That makes a discounted free-cash-flow model the primary method, and it is the only method we weight. We do not weight a P/E leg, and the reason is mechanical rather than aesthetic: the engine applies any peer multiple to last-twelve-month earnings per share of Rp90, which is about half the earning power our FY2026E estimate of Rp153 carries. Presented that way a multiple-based value is a floor, not a value. We keep the dividend-yield leg out for the same reason — capitalising the forward dividend at a peer market yield uses a market yield rather than a required return. Both remain visible as cross-checks through the peer table and the multiples below [S3, S0].

The cost of equity is 12.9%, and the build is exact: a risk-free rate of 7.4% less the 1.6% sovereign default spread embedded in the local ten-year yield, plus a levered beta of 1.06 times the mature-market equity risk premium plus the country risk premium of 2.5%. The unlevered beta of 0.70 is levered at the group's debt-to-equity of 0.65. That is how 12.9% is reproduced. WACC uses the market pre-tax cost of debt, 9.4% (risk-free plus the house corporate spread), and the weights implied by that same debt-to-equity, giving 10.7% [S0, S3].

The cost of debt needs a sentence of its own because the company pays less than the market rate. The interest line runs at 7.2%, the effective rate on the actual book; the discount rate runs at 9.4%, the rate a marginal borrower would pay. These are two different questions, not two answers to the same one. The book is short-term bank debt priced off the policy rate and repriced annually, and part of it is older and relationship-priced, so the contracted rate is below the marginal rate [S3]. Discounting the perpetuity at the contracted rate would subsidise it; expensing next year's P&L at the marginal rate would overstate the interest actually payable. We disclose the choice and its direction: using the contracted rate in WACC would lower the discount rate and raise the DCF, and we do not take that value because it is not a rate the company could refinance at.

The DCF gives Rp1,524 a share, an enterprise value of IDR3,448.6bn with 48.6% of it in the terminal value. The first forecast year is a half-year stub measured from the 30 June balance sheet; the valuation bridge carries the working-capital correction described in the financial section, so that H2 bears the build to the 8.0% target from the June position rather than a release, and that correction is the single largest adjustment in this model [S0]. The terminal assumptions are funded, not declared: growth of 3.0%, below nominal GDP, with terminal capex at 5.45% of sales against D&A of 4.35% and working capital at 8.0% of sales. Net reinvestment works out at about a quarter of NOPAT; at a terminal return on capital in the low teens that funds exactly 3.0%. Set growth at nominal GDP with capex equal to D&A and you would be assuming growth for free. At the terminal year the implied exit EV/EBIT is below the multiple the market is paying for the business today, so this is not multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume.

**The peer cross-check.** The table below is the peer set we pinned — the IDX staples complex, not the micro-cap household names the config would otherwise pull in — with each peer's trailing multiples and the median [S0].

At Rp1,570 the market pays 10.3x our FY2026E earnings and 5.7x EV/EBITDA; the peer median on the table is higher than that on EV/EBITDA and about level on P/E. Our target of Rp1,345 implies a lower multiple than today's on both, because the target is the discounted, liquidity-haircut value and we assume no re-rating: the target does not require the shares to trade at the peer median, and a buyer at the target pays less than the peer median for a business with a thinner float and a policy risk the larger names do not carry. The apparent cheapness on P/E is the one-off in FY2026 earnings; on FY2027E the multiple is 10.6x against a lower earnings base, which is why we do not lean on the P/E comparison. The EV/EBITDA discount to peers is real, and leverage and float explain most of it [S3, S0]. A re-rating to the peer median is an upside we leave to the bull case, not a component of the target.

The forward view is where the tension sits: the shares look cheap on the earnings we forecast and close to fair on the cash the business will actually release once reinvestment and the first-year working-capital build are paid for. That is the whole argument of this note, and it is why the target is close to the price rather than a re-rating call.

The value is most sensitive to gross margin and to the cost base, then to the discount rate. The illiquidity discount of 20.0% is applied on top of the fundamental value, and it is derived from turnover alone: three-month average daily value traded is IDR133.9m, which sits below the half-billion-rupiah threshold and above the hundred-million-rupiah floor — the band that carries that discount regardless of the float [S0]. The public float itself is 13.5% with 3.5% in treasury [S3]; that is small, but the discount rests on the turnover, not on a round-number float claim. It is the difference between a fundamental value close to the price and a target below it.

**What the price implies.** Running the model backwards, today's price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of 8.4% against the 8.0% we forecast. So the market is not pricing a heroic recovery; it is pricing slightly less growth than we assume and applying its own liquidity discount. The rolling convention is worth stating: the DCF is a present value at the report date, it is rolled twelve months at the cost of equity to the target date, and the next twelve months' dividend of Rp76 is deducted because the buyer of the shares does not receive it before the target date.

**Regulatory — the excise (high likelihood, high impact).** The MBDK excise is committed for H2-2027 with the rate and sugar threshold unset [S4, S6]. Beverages are 53.0% of revenue [S3]. A rate set high enough to change consumer prices materially would hit volumes in the segment that carries the group, and reformulation takes time. This is the single largest identified risk and the reason our FY2027 growth assumption is below FY2026's.

**Liquidity and covenants (medium likelihood, high impact).** This is the risk the filings name most plainly, and it is both a liquidity and a leverage story. The FY2025 current ratio was below the 1.0x covenant — current assets of IDR1,580.5bn against current liabilities of IDR2,375.9bn — and the company needed waivers from CIMB, CTBC, OCBC and BCA, dated between 20 February and 30 March 2026, for non-fulfilment of FY2025 financial covenants including the current ratio [S3]. The leverage covenant is the thin one rather than the broken one: at the same test date interest-bearing debt of IDR1,561.3bn is three point seven times restated EBITDA of IDR417.2bn, and net debt of IDR1,437.6bn is 3.4x restated EBITDA, against the 4.0x limit [S0, S3]. The waivers do not settle whether that test was breached: CTBC's approval names the minimum current ratio, while CIMB, OCBC and BCA approve non-fulfilment of the FY2025 financial covenants without saying which, so we treat the leverage line as close, not as comfortably passed. Four times that EBITDA is the ceiling, so the FY2025 balance sat about a quarter of a turn — of the order of a hundred billion rupiah, roughly a six per cent cushion — inside it. A filer that needed covenant waivers at that leverage is not a comfortable credit: a weak second half, a rupiah-driven margin squeeze or a bank pulling a short-term line could put the leverage test itself at risk, and that is why we do not treat the covenant as a non-issue. We model the repair rather than assume it — net debt to EBITDA falls to 2.1x and interest-bearing debt to EBITDA to about two and a half times in FY2026E — so the cushion widens on our numbers rather than staying where it was. Interest expense was IDR129.3bn against EBIT of IDR213.1bn in FY2025 [S0].

**Input costs and the rupiah (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Raw and packaging materials are the bulk of cost of goods sold and part of the bill is imported [S3]. Pass-through is good but not complete; a simultaneous CPO and rupiah move compresses gross margin by more than our cost link assumes.

**Execution of the margin recovery (medium likelihood, high impact).** The earnings inflection rests on operating leverage: the same revenue with a smaller cost ratio. If the first half's promotion discipline was a timing effect, the second half gives it back and the FY2026 EBITDA margin of 11.4% is not achieved [S0].

**Liquidity in the shares (certain, high impact).** A 13.5% public float and 85.3% insider ownership, with a founder who is also the president director [S0, S3], mean the price is set at the margin by a small number of holders. Average daily turnover of IDR133.9m means a large seller can move the stock well below fundamental value and a buyer cannot accumulate without doing the same in reverse. The illiquidity discount in the target is the quantified cost of that — the turnover sits in the band that carries it, and the corrected figure leaves the discount unchanged — and it is also why a placing that raised the float would be a positive event.

**Governance (low likelihood, medium impact).** A controlled company with a mid-tier auditor [S3] and related-party balances to a common-control entity [S3]; nothing manipulation-class found, but minority holders have limited influence.

Bear (probability 25.0%, value Rp558): the excise is set high, volume in beverages falls and promotion spending rises to defend share, so the margin recovery reverses; costs and interest stay high and earnings return toward the FY2025 level. Bull (20.0%, Rp3,187): the excise is set low and passed through, the first-half momentum holds, gross margin stays near the top of the range and debt repayment shrinks the interest line, so earnings compound ahead of sales. Base (55.0%, Rp1,645) is the path we have described: growth fading from the 2026 step to mid-single digits, margins held at the achieved level, debt repaid on the observed schedule.

The probabilities are set on likelihood, not symmetry. The base gets the majority because it is the last actual reproduced at that year's prices and the company's own plan, with the excise a year away and its rate unset. The bear gets a quarter: the policy risk is committed and would land on the majority of sales, but it needs a high rate, weak pass-through and a margin reversal together. The bull gets a fifth: it needs a low rate, the margin to hold and faster deleveraging at once. The shock sizes are mirrored — revenue growth moved by the same amount in each direction and gross margin by the same amount in each direction — so the wide spread in values is not a lopsided scenario; it is the operating and financial leverage of the business, which magnifies any margin move in both directions. If the bear and base probabilities were reversed, the weighted value would fall below the current price, which is precisely why we are not buyers here.

**Signposts that would change our view:** the third-quarter operating margin (does the first half hold?); the excise implementing regulation (rate and sugar threshold); the FY2026 audited D&A and EBITDA; the interest-bearing-debt-to-EBITDA ratio at the FY2026 test date — the FY2025 cushion was a quarter of a turn, so any EBITDA disappointment moves it back toward the limit; the current ratio at the next year-end and whether a waiver is needed again; any change in the free float — a placing by the controlling shareholder would cut the liquidity discount and could turn this into a BUY on the same fundamentals; and the dividend at the FY2026 results [S3, S4].

Kino is controlled by PT Kino Investindo with 79.0% of the shares; the founder, Harry Sanusi, is both a direct holder and president director, the public holds 13.5% and a treasury stake of 3.5% is held [S3]. The free float is small — below the threshold that would make the stock eligible for most institutional mandates and the origin of the valuation discount — but it is larger than the data pack's figure, which is why we use the annual report's register [S3, S0]. There are no pledged-share disclosures in the annual report or the announcements we reviewed, and no rights issue or private placement has been done since listing [S3, S2]. A discounted placement to an affiliate would be the flag to watch in a company with this ownership structure; none has occurred.

Related-party dealings are small and operational: other payables to PT Royal Bintang Persada, an entity under common control, for lease and interest expense, at IDR7.5bn against total liabilities of IDR2,722.2bn [S3]. The material-transaction section of the FY2025 report lists no conflicted transaction of size [S3]. The auditor is Mirawati Sensi Idris, a mid-tier practice [S3]; the accounts carry an unqualified opinion and the audit committee is chaired by an independent commissioner [S3]. The commissioner side of the board is majority independent, with the founder as president director — normal for a family-controlled IDX mid-cap, and a real constraint on minority influence.

The dividend record is the strongest governance signal: the payout has risen in each of the last two years, to Rp45 a share for FY2025, 50.2% of net profit [S3, S0]. A controlling family that pays out half its earnings while deleveraging is not extracting value through related-party channels. The covenant waivers are a governance disclosure positive as well: they are named, dated and explained in the accounts rather than left for the reader to find [S3].

ESG exposures specific to this company: packaging intensity across the segments, sugar content in beverages — exactly what the excise targets [S4] — water use at the plants, which the annual report describes as treated in-house [S3], and palm-derived inputs, where the sustainability question is passed up the supply chain. The FY2025 report carries a separate sustainability report and a supplier code [S3]. None of these is currently a valuation driver outside the excise; the excise is the one that is.

The dated catalysts are the nine-month 2026 results at the end of November, the FY2026 audited accounts and the FY2027 dividend proposal in the first quarter of 2027, the excise implementing regulation targeted before mid-2027, and the start of the excise regime in the second half of 2027 [S4, S3].

The KPIs we watch between updates: quarterly revenue growth and the split between volume and price; selling expense as a share of sales, where the margin recovery lives; gross margin against the CPO and packaging basket; interest expense and the debt balance; operating cash flow against net profit; the dividend per share and payout; and any change in the free float or the shareholder register [S3, S0].

Two things would make us more positive without any change in the fundamentals: a placing that lifts the free float and with it removes part of the illiquidity discount, and an excise rate set low enough that it is a pricing event rather than a volume event [S4]. Two would make us negative: a first half that turns out to be the peak margin, and a refinancing at a higher rate than the 7.2% we carry [S3].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for KINO.JK

S4.title: Cukai Minuman Manis Ditargetkan Berlaku Semester II-2027, Tarif Masih Dibahas

bear.narrative: The excise on sweetened packaged drinks lands in H2-2027 at a rate that has to be absorbed on a business where beverages are 53% of sales; volume dips and promotion spending rises, so the 2026H1 margin recovery reverses. Costs keep rising faster than prices and the short-term bank lines reprice higher, leaving profit near FY2025 levels.

bull.narrative: The excise is set low and passed through; beverages and pet food keep the 2026H1 momentum, gross margin holds near 44% and the fixed cost base spreads further. Debt keeps falling, so the interest line shrinks and earnings compound well ahead of sales.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026 anchors on the actual half-year: 2026H1 sales grew 21.7% y/y (Rp2,629.98bn vs Rp2,159.98bn; pack quarters, cross-checked against FY2025 revenue of Rp4,421.55bn) [S0, S3], which already beats the board's cautious "in line with ~5% GDP growth" 2026 projection [S3]. We carry 18.5% for FY2026 (H2 assumed +15% on a tougher base) and then 8.0-8.5% nominal, the growth the company's own FY2025 report calls the domestic FMCG norm, with FY2027 trimmed to 8.0% for the sweetened-beverage excise landing in H2-2027 on a 53% beverages business [S4, S3]. Terminal 4.5% = long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin 43.55% (gross profit Rp1,925.67bn on sales Rp4,421.55bn) [S3]; 2026H1 is 43.58% (Rp1,145.87bn on Rp2,629.98bn) [S0], so the first half shows no mix or price erosion. Held flat at the last actual rather than faded: management's stated response to input inflation is to raise selling prices and to dual-source raw and packaging materials [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: CPO is a proxy basket, not a disclosed line: it stands for palm-derived surfactants and glycerine in personal care plus plastic packaging across all five segments. Raw and packaging materials are the bulk of cost of goods sold (manufacturing overhead, depreciation and direct labour aside) and the company names raw-material and packaging-price risk as its principal operating exposure [S3]. We put one fifth of COGS on the palm-and-packaging basket.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: High pass-through: the FY2025 report states that when raw and packaging costs rise "one way the Company addresses it is by raising selling prices", and that the whole industry faces the same input inflation [S3]. Brand-led pricing in sachet and masstige categories supports most of the move; we leave a fifth of the shock in the margin.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling plus general-and-administrative expense was 38.3% of sales (Rp1,356.94bn + Rp338.23bn) [S3], but 2026H1 already runs at 36.3% (gross profit Rp1,145.87bn less EBIT Rp192.42bn on Rp2,629.98bn of sales) [S0]: the fixed part of the cost base is being spread over 22% more revenue. We hold the achieved 2026H1 ratio rather than revert to FY2025, which would model away an actual.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated D&A of Rp204.01bn for FY2025 is 4.61% of sales [S3, facts F3]; held at 4.60% then eased to 4.35% as the FY2025 revaluation-related depreciation base is not repeated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex Rp208.11bn, 4.71% of sales, up 63% on the prior year as the group bought plant [S3]. Near term capex tracks D&A: utilisation is low (personal care 15.9% of 84,259 kl installed capacity, beverages under 70%), so 8% growth needs little new capacity [S3]. From FY2029 we lift capex above D&A because growth is manufactured (VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY §1). The terminal rate is set by the terminal growth it has to fund, not the other way round: with terminal NOPAT at 5.37% of sales (6.8% EBIT margin, 21% tax), capex at 5.45% against D&A at 4.35% and working capital at 8% of a 3.0% growth rate, net reinvestment is 1.34% of sales = 25% of NOPAT; at a terminal ROIC of 12% that funds g = 25% x 12% = 3.0%. A 5.2% terminal capex would fund only about 2.4% and a capex-equals-D&A terminal would assume growth for free.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was Rp455.82bn at FY2025 (10.3% of sales) and Rp318.50bn at 2026-06-30 (6.1% of run-rate sales), the release behind FY2025 operating cash flow of Rp632.17bn versus net profit of Rp125.93bn [S0, S3]. We set 8.0%, between the two actuals, so the model does not assume the release keeps repeating. Because the forecast year is a half-year stub from 30 June, the FY2026E change is corrected in valuation.bridge: the target NWC of 8% of FY2026 sales is Rp419.16bn against the Rp318.50bn already on the June balance sheet, so H2 must BUILD Rp100.66bn, not release part of the year.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate 20.5% (tax Rp32.43bn on pre-tax profit Rp158.35bn) [S3], just under the 22% statutory rate; the three-year default of 23.1% is distorted by FY2022 losses.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Two rates, each with a stated job, and no third. The interest line uses the rate the company actually pays: FY2025 interest expense Rp129.34bn on opening interest-bearing debt of Rp1,783.13bn = 7.25%, and 2026H1 expense of Rp54.05bn on average debt of about Rp1,489bn is 7.26% [S3, S0] — the last actual, held. The discount rate uses the rate a marginal borrower pays: rf 7.45% plus the house 2.00pp corporate spread = 9.45% pre-tax, which is the engine's kd_pre_tax and is used only in WACC. The company's book is short-term bank lines (CIMB, CTBC, OCBC, BCA) priced off the policy rate and repriced annually [S3]; the effective 7.25% is below the marginal rate because part of the book is older and relationship-priced. Discounting at the contracted rate would subsidise the perpetuity; the P&L at the market rate would overstate the interest actually payable next year. The difference is disclosed in section 4 rather than averaged away.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income Rp1.88bn on opening cash of Rp121.21bn = 1.55% [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Deleveraging path: interest-bearing debt fell from Rp1,783.13bn to Rp1,561.31bn in FY2025 and to Rp1,417.04bn by 2026-06-30 [S0, S3]. Repayment is the company's observed behaviour, not an upside to leave out: we model net repayment of Rp72bn in the H2-2026 stub (a Rp144bn annual pace, close to FY2025's), tapering to Rp60bn by FY2030 and nil in the terminal year, so gross debt falls from Rp1,417bn to about Rp0.9trn and the interest line shrinks with it instead of cash piling up at a deposit yield below the cost of debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: 2026H1 EBIT was Rp192.43bn, net interest expense Rp52.88bn (interest expense Rp54.05bn less interest income Rp1.17bn) and pre-tax profit Rp152.59bn, so other non-operating items netted to +Rp13.05bn in the half — pre-tax sits BELOW EBIT by the net interest charge, not level with it [S0]. Annualised that is about Rp26bn, which is what we carry in FY2026 only, and nil after, because it is not an operating earnings stream; it is why FY2026 net profit is above FY2027's on a clean basis. FY2025 shows the same reconciliation: EBIT plus a net +Rp72.67bn of other income (FX gains, a trademark impairment charge and disposal items the company groups as non-operating) less net interest gives pre-tax profit of Rp158.35bn [S0, S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities took Rp2.23bn of Rp125.93bn net profit, 1.8%, after the first-stage liquidation of a subsidiary [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp45 a share (Rp62.0bn, ~50% of FY2025 net profit of Rp123.70bn), up from Rp32 for FY2024 (49.6% of that year's profit) and Rp22 for FY2023 [S3, S0]. We hold the last actual 49.6% rather than step it down to 45%: the ratchet has moved up, not down.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 1,378.819m shares outstanding; treasury 3.48% held, no issuance assumed [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%: funded by the reinvestment the model actually carries, not asserted. Terminal capex is 5.45% of sales against D&A of 4.35% and working capital at 8% of sales growing 3.0% (0.24pp), so net reinvestment is 1.34% of sales; terminal NOPAT is 5.37% of sales (6.8% EBIT margin, 21% tax). That is a 25% reinvestment rate; at a terminal ROIC of 12% it funds g = 25% x 12% = 3.0% (VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY §1). Terminal g is inside the 2.5-5% cap for IDR revenue and below nominal GDP. A 3.5% rate would have required either a higher reinvestment rate or a higher terminal return than this business has earned.

challenges.challenge: The Rp45.0bn FY2026 non-operating income is justified by 'implied pre-tax profit Rp196bn on EBIT Rp192bn' in 2026H1, and section 3 states 'pre-tax profit roughly equals EBIT'. The pack's own quarters show 2026Q1 PBT 61.61 + Q2 90.98 = 152.59bn against EBIT 192.43bn: pre-tax is Rp40bn BELOW EBIT, not equal to it. The item is 15% of FY2026E net profit, creates the FY2026 234.6 > FY2027 209.6 decline, and underpins the 9.2x FY2026E earnings claim.
challenges.answer: Other non-operating income cut to Rp26.1bn, the annualised 2026H1 run-rate, in FY2026 only and nil afterwards [S0]. Section 3 now builds pre-tax profit as EBIT less net interest plus other income using placeholders, states that 2026H1 pre-tax sat below EBIT, and explains that FY2026 net profit exceeds FY2027 only because that one-off disappears. The 45bn line and the pre-tax-equals-EBIT sentence are gone.

challenges.challenge: Facts F3/F4 carry D&A of Rp204.01bn (FY2025) and Rp206.55bn (FY2024) on a PY2025 quote that shows the PPE depreciation total as Rp168.0526bn (and Rp161.2619bn for FY2024), Note 11 p280. The report's extra Rp36bn of right-of-use depreciation and intangible amortisation is asserted, not cited. D&A is half of FCFF and the basis of the EBITDA, leverage and 3.4x net-debt/EBITDA narrative.
challenges.answer: The extra Rp36bn is now cited line by line: right-of-use depreciation of Rp11.70bn in selling expense and Rp16.92bn in administrative expense, plus intangible amortisation of Rp7.34bn, on top of PPE depreciation of Rp168.05bn [S3]. Facts F20, F21 and F22 carry the verbatim quotes and the total reconciles to the restated DA; EBIT and FCFF are unchanged.

challenges.challenge: The same debt is priced three ways: WACC kd 9.45% (rf 7.45 + 2.0 spread), the interest line 6.5%, and the FY2025 effective 7.25% (H1-2026 run-rate 108/1,417 = 7.6%). The report also writes 'pre-tax cost of debt at 9.4% - the FY2025 effective rate marked down toward the policy rate', which is false in both direction and level. Separately, the COE build as printed (7.4% plus a default spread, 1.06 x (4.2+2.5)) gives 14.5%, not 12.9%: the engine subtracts the 1.62pp spread and the note omits it.
challenges.answer: The COE paragraph is rewritten with the exact build: 7.45% less the 1.62pp default spread plus 1.057 levered beta times 6.69% gives 12.90%; the old 14.5% reading and the false marked-down-debt sentence are deleted. One rate per job, labelled: 7.25% effective on the P&L interest line and 9.45% marginal in WACC, with the direction of the gap disclosed rather than averaged.

challenges.challenge: The DCF is struck at 30-Jun-2026 (FY2026 row fraction 0.504, discounted at time zero) but FY2026 FCFF carries a full-year working-capital release of Rp36.7bn, against an FY2025 NWC of Rp455.8bn. NWC was already Rp318.5bn at 30 June per the note's own basis, so the correct H2-2026 movement to the 8%-of-sales target (Rp419.2bn) is a BUILD of Rp100.7bn, not the Rp18.5bn release embedded in the stub. That overstates H2 FCFF by about Rp119bn, roughly 5% of equity value (Rp86/share).
challenges.answer: The FY2026 stub is corrected explicitly: the 8% target NWC at FY2026 sales is Rp419.16bn against Rp318.50bn already on the 30 June sheet, so H2 must build Rp100.66bn. A valuation bridge item of minus Rp119.15bn removes the full-year release embedded in the stub, worth about Rp86 per share, and sections 3 and 4 state the basis.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth is 3.5% but the note's own reinvestment arithmetic gives 2.4-3.0% (reinvestment about 20% of NOPAT x ROIC about 12%); the basis text itself says 'supports roughly 2.5-3%' and then sets 3.5%. Terminal value is 51.3% of EV, so 100bp of g is about 12% of TV and 6% of EV, roughly Rp110-120/share of value created without capital.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth stays at 3.0% but is now funded by the model: terminal capex is lifted to 5.45% of sales against DA of 4.35%, so net reinvestment is 1.34% of sales, a quarter of NOPAT, and at a terminal ROIC in the low teens it funds exactly 3.0%. The basis and section 4 show the arithmetic; the 3.5% claim is gone.

challenges.challenge: The payout is set at 45% although the note itself states the FY2025 dividend was about 50% of profit and AR2025 p123 shows FY2024 at 49.62% (Rp32/share on Rp44.12bn) and FY2023 at 39.27%, a rising ratchet. There is no source for the 5pp haircut, and the prose says 'about 0.5' immediately before modelling 0.45. It understates DPS and the 4.9% yield claim (5.4% at 50%).
challenges.answer: The payout is held at the last actual 49.6% in all forecast years instead of 45%; the prose already argued the ratchet and now matches the model. DPS, the dividend yield and the DPS deducted in the twelve-month roll all move with it [S3, S0].

challenges.challenge: The 20% illiquidity discount is justified by a '9.0% free float' and 'a few hundred million rupiah' of daily turnover. AR2025 p76 shows public 192,458,843 shares = 13.48% and treasury 3.48%; the model's ADTV is Rp134m/day, not a few hundred million. The float is understated by a third, and the discount is therefore resting on a wrong fact, even if Rp134m/day independently justifies some discount. A second conservatism: the DCF value dates from 30 June but is rolled only 12 months to 30 June 2027 against a 6 November price date, and a full next-12m DPS of 77 is deducted from that shorter period - about 4% (Rp80/share) of understatement.
challenges.answer: Float corrected to the register: public 13.48% (fact F26) with treasury 3.48% stated separately (F27), replacing the data pack 9.0%. The security-specific discount is derived from ADTV alone: Rp134m a day sits in the second house band and drives 20% regardless of float. The roll is rebutted on mechanics: v0 is discounted to the report date, rolled twelve months at COE, with dps12 deducted for the buyer.

challenges.challenge: At base 50 / bear 25 / bull 25 the weighted value is Rp2,119 and the bull contributes Rp913bn, 43% of it; the bull is 2.0x the base value and 4.4x the bear. At base 40 / bear 50 / bull 10, a defensible reading for a name whose largest policy risk is committed for H2-2027 and unpriced in rate terms, the target is about Rp1,262, below the market price. The summary also says the target is the DCF 'rolled forward at the cost of equity and then cut by 20%', which describes only the base path (1,997 x 0.8 = 1,598) and omits the probability weighting that lifts it to 1,695.
challenges.answer: The summary now shows the full build: DCF to base value, rolled to the twelve-month target, scenario-weighted at 55/25/20, then the 20% discount to the final target. Probabilities are justified on likelihood, not symmetry: the bear needs a high excise rate, weak pass-through and a margin reversal together; the bull needs a low rate, margin hold and faster deleveraging. Mirrored shocks and the leverage-driven value spread are explained, and the report says reversing bear and base puts the value below the price.

challenges.challenge: The note says the FY2025 test date required a covenant waiver 'in February 2026' and treats it as a leverage near-miss. AR2025 p129 records the CIMB waiver as No. 011/SK/COBA-CBTV-NT/III/2026 dated 11 March 2026 for non-fulfilment of financial covenants for FY2025 'including Current Ratio', plus a separate CTBC waiver. The month is wrong, the scope is understated, and the covenant actually named is a liquidity test, not debt/EBITDA. No covenant level or headroom figure is given anywhere.
challenges.answer: Covenant section corrected to the accounts: four waivers, CIMB 11 March, CTBC 30 March with a minimum current ratio of 1.0x, OCBC 20 February and BCA 13 March 2026 [S3]. The covenant levels are now facts F31-F34 (current ratio 1.0x, IBD/equity 2.5x, IBD/EBITDA 4x, DSCR 1.0x), the breach is treated as a liquidity risk with FY2025 current assets and liabilities stated, and FY2026E IBD/EBITDA headroom is shown. The February date and leverage framing are gone.

challenges.challenge: Deleveraging is the clearest company-specific upside and it is nowhere in the base or bull case. Debt fell Rp1,783bn to Rp1,561bn in FY2025 and to Rp1,417bn by June 2026; the model assumes zero net repayment forever and lets cash reach Rp1.17trn at a 1.55% yield while paying 6.5% on Rp1.56trn of debt, an economic loss of about Rp57bn a year by FY2035 that no management would tolerate. Each Rp100bn repaid saves about Rp6.5bn pre-tax. Also unvalued: a control-block transaction at 79% ownership, and any cancellation of the 3.48% treasury stake.
challenges.answer: Deleveraging is now in the base case, not just the prose: net repayment of Rp72bn in the H2-2026 stub, Rp144bn in FY2027 tapering to Rp60bn by FY2030, so debt falls and interest expense drops from FY2025 129.3 to FY2030 61.2; cash no longer accumulates at the deposit yield. Treasury cancellation and a control-block sale are flagged as unvalued optionality without a number.

challenges.challenge: The structure-flag screen stops at 'the auditor is a mid-tier firm' and never considers a discounted placement or rights issue to an affiliate - the modal IDX value-destruction channel - despite 79% control, 13.48% public float, 0.99x book and a balance sheet that has just needed covenant waivers. The related-party item is dismissed at 'about one per cent of liabilities' when Rp7.5bn against Rp2,722bn of liabilities is 0.28%.
challenges.answer: Structure screen completed: no pledge disclosure, no rights issue or private placement, no pending issuance, auditor mid-tier with an unqualified opinion (S3, S2). The related-party ratio is corrected to Rp7.5bn against total liabilities of Rp2,722bn, which is 0.28% of liabilities, not about one per cent; the fact and placeholder carry both numbers.

challenges.challenge: The pinned peer set is never shown. The model's own peers give a median P/E of 10.3x (n=8) and EV/EBITDA of 7.62x; Kino enters at 9.2x FY2026E and 5.7x, and at the target is still only about 5.96x EV/EBITDA, a 22% discount to peers. That is a real cross-check and an upside the note asserts ('cheap against the IDX staples complex') but never quantifies, while calling the target multiple a 'low-teens forward earnings multiple' when it is 10.0x FY2026E and 11.2x FY2027E.
challenges.answer: The pinned peer set is now shown in table:peers with each peer trailing multiple and the median, plus table:multiples. The note states the target-implied multiple on both P/E and EV/EBITDA sits below today and below the peer median, explains the P/E gap by the FY2026 one-off, shows FY2027E P/E, and says explicitly that no re-rating is in the target.

challenges.challenge: Unit and transcription errors sit in load-bearing paragraphs: 'IDR22.0bn a share' for FY2023 (AR p123 shows Rp22/share, Rp30.33bn total), '13,420 kl kl' and '11,490,232 kg kg', 'the policy rate at 5.8 rate', and the dividend paragraph mixing per-share and total-rupiah units.
challenges.answer: Units fixed throughout: per-share figures use the ps format, fact placeholders render their own units so the duplicated kl and kg tokens are gone, the policy-rate sentence is rewritten from the deck placeholder, and the dividend paragraph now uses per-share values consistently [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 states that on the restated measure interest-bearing debt to EBITDA sits at 2.1x against the 4.0x covenant and that the leverage test has headroom. FY2025 interest-bearing debt of Rp1,561.3bn over restated EBITDA of Rp417.2bn is 3.74x, and section 3 prints net debt of Rp1,437.6bn as 3.4x restated EBITDA. The 2.1x figure understates covenant pressure by 1.6 turns on a filer that obtained current-ratio waivers from CIMB, CTBC, OCBC and BCA for the FY2025 test date.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now states interest-bearing debt of Rp1,561.3bn at three point seven times restated EBITDA of Rp417.2bn and net debt at 3.4x against the 4.0x limit, gives the cushion as a quarter of a turn (about a hundred billion rupiah, roughly six per cent of the covenant band), notes that three of the four waivers are generic on FY2025 financial covenants so the leverage test cannot be assumed untouched, and rewrites the conclusion to say the covenant is thin rather than comfortable; section 3 labels its forward 2.1x as net debt/EBITDA and adds the test-date ratio [S3, S0]

challenges.challenge: The section 3 restatement sentence cannot be right as printed: it gives IDR204.0bn as PPE depreciation before the other components, adds right-of-use depreciation of 11.7bn and 16.9bn and intangible amortisation of 7.3bn, and then states a total of IDR204.0bn. A reader cannot tell which figure was restated or how the components sum.
challenges.answer: The restatement now shows the four components that sum: PPE depreciation IDR168.1bn plus right-of-use depreciation of IDR11.7bn in selling and IDR16.9bn in administration plus amortisation of IDR7.3bn equals the IDR204.0bn restated D&A, and FY2024 is built the same way from IDR161.3bn, IDR17.4bn, IDR17.5bn and IDR10.4bn to IDR206.6bn [S3]

challenges.challenge: Section 5 prints average daily turnover of IDR133,939,881.0bn, which reads as Rp134 trillion and is about a thousand times any plausible figure for a name with a 13.5% float. The liquidity discount in the target is justified on that paragraph.
challenges.answer: The money filter on market fields is fixed: turnover prints as IDR133.9m a day, which sits below the half-billion-rupiah threshold and above the hundred-million-rupiah floor, so the twenty per cent band still applies and the discount is unchanged; the float sentence around it is restated on that figure [S0]

challenges.challenge: The terminal-capex token in the terminal-growth paragraph points at the FY2030E rate of 5.3%, while the terminal_growth basis funds 3.0% from a terminal capex of 5.45% of sales against D&A of 4.35%. The reinvestment arithmetic a reader checks is therefore shown with the wrong input.
challenges.answer: The terminal paragraph now points at the FY2035E capex ratio of 5.45% of sales and D&A of 4.35%, matching the terminal_growth basis that funds 3.0% from a twenty-five per cent reinvestment rate at a twelve per cent terminal return on capital [S3, S0]

findings.finding: The investment summary prints an 8.0% free-cash-flow-to-equity yield from mult.FY2026E.fcfe_yield, but that line contains the Rp126.9bn FY2025-to-FY2026 working-capital release that the valuation bridge itself reverses with a -Rp119.2bn stub correction; after that correction FY2026 FCFE is about Rp51bn (2.4%) and the engine FY2027E yield is 1.1%. The 8.0% is a one-off, not the recurring cash yield, yet it is used to argue the shares are not expensive.

Section 5 says 85.3% insider ownership from mkt.insider_pct (S0 data pack), but the S3 register it also cites shows PT Kino Investindo 79.00% plus Harry Sanusi 4.04% = 83.04% insider, 13.48% public and 3.48% treasury; 85.3% plus 13.5% plus 3.5% exceeds 100%. The same register shows control rising from 70.00% in 2024 to 79.00% in 2025 while public fell from 22.48% to 13.48%, which the governance section does not explain.

Section 4 says the peer median is higher than that on EV/EBITDA and about level on P/E and refers to apparent cheapness on P/E. The pinned nine-peer table gives median trailing P/E of 9.03x against Kino at 10.27x FY2026E (a 14% premium) and median EV/EBITDA of 6.97x against 5.73x (an 18% discount). The P/E sentence is stale from the earlier eight-peer set whose median was 10.3x and now contradicts the table.

Section 3 FY2026 bridge reads net interest of IDR113.2bn, other income of IDR26.1bn and pre-tax of IDR271.8bn, but 357.0 - 113.2 + 26.1 = 269.9. The engine interest_expense is 113.2 and interest_income 1.9, so the stated PBT of 271.8 requires net interest of 111.3; the FY2025 sentence carries the same gross-versus-net mislabel (round-1 Q6, still open).

The terminal_growth basis funds 3.0% from a 6.8% EBIT margin and 5.37% NOPAT, but the model FY2035E EBIT margin is 6.37% (EBIT 565.69 on revenue 8,883.01) and NOPAT 5.03%, so reinvestment is 26.6% of NOPAT and implied terminal ROIC is 11.3%. The rendered about-a-quarter wording remains fair; the basis numbers should be aligned [S0].

The covenant sentence rests on restated EBITDA of IDR417.2bn built on the data-pack EBIT of IDR213.1bn. The audited P&L gives operating profit of IDR230.5bn before ECL of 19.2 and bank administration of 6.2, so a filing-only EBITDA is about IDR409-411bn and the FY2025 ratio is about 3.8x rather than 3.7x, still inside 4.0x with roughly a fifth to a quarter of a turn of headroom.

The 2026H1 sales basis prints Rp2,629.98bn; the pack quarters sum to Rp2,628.98bn (1,256.02 + 1,372.96), a Rp1bn slip that does not change the 21.7% growth. The payout basis still calls 49.6% the last actual: FY2025 is 50.2% on parent net profit, while 49.6% is the FY2024 total-profit ratio (round-1 Q6).

Judge NOTE adopted: the -72 net_borrowing is described as an H2-2026 stub but the engine applies it to FY2026 as a whole, so modelled year-end debt of Rp1,489.31bn is above the June actual of Rp1,417.04bn and interest is charged on the FY2025 opening balance; about Rp10bn pre-tax conservative, with no FCFF effect (round-1 Q7).
